text: It didn't look like a submarine. It looked like a giant metal balloon, because that's basically what it was. A huge float filled with petrol, which is lighter than water, and hanging underneath it, a small steel ball for the crew.
Inside that ball were two men: Swiss engineer Jacques Piccard and U.S. Navy officer Don Walsh.
On the twenty-third of January, 1960, they began sinking into the Challenger Deep.
The descent took almost five hours. It was cold. It was cramped. And at around nine kilometres down...
...there was a loud bang. The whole sphere shook.
One of the outer windows had cracked. With a thousand atmospheres waiting outside.
They checked their instruments. The sphere was holding. So they made a decision that still sounds crazy today. They kept going.
And they touched the bottom. The first humans ever to reach the deepest place on Earth.
They stayed for about twenty minutes. The landing had stirred up a cloud of fine mud, so they could barely see. Then they started the long ride back up.
[shaking his head, smiling] Deepest picnic in history.
Then... nobody went back. For fifty-two years.

In 2012, film director James Cameron, the man who made Titanic, dived down alone in a narrow green sub called the Deepsea Challenger. Since then, a few more explorers have made it, including Victor Vescovo, the man who found that plastic bag.
Think about that. Twelve people have walked on the Moon. Until 2019, only three had ever been to the Challenger Deep.
And when they got there, they found something nobody expected.
